name: Posture for height (rib/pelvic tilt)
lead: Posture for height is the practice of working on pelvic tilt, rib flare and related alignment patterns in the hope of standing taller, looking leaner through the midsection and carrying the body with a more upright, proportioned look. In looksmaxxing communities it is one of the most frequently raised height topics: threads ask whether correcting anterior pelvic tilt (APT) adds inches, how to fix it, and whether tilted shoulders or hips relate to facial asymmetry.[1][2][3][10][11] Because it uses ordinary stretching, strengthening and movement work, it is often treated as a first, low-cost step before more involved height or physique methods.

The idea rests on how the pelvis and spine are stacked. When the front of the pelvis tips down, the lower back arches more, the belly and buttocks can appear pushed out, and the head and shoulders often shift to compensate. Proponents say undoing this pattern lets a person stand to the height their skeleton allows and look more balanced. Wikipedia describes anterior, posterior and lateral pelvic tilt with the muscle patterns and exercises usually associated with each, and illustrates the article with an image suggesting posture can change apparent height.[4] Clinical research on pelvic tilt is mostly about spinal alignment, pain and disability in patients rather than stature in healthy people.[5][6][8]

chain: Stretch tight hip flexors and strengthen glutes and core
Pelvis and lower-back curve move toward a neutral stack
Standing and measured height may rise a little, and the midsection, back and shoulder line look more upright
angle.text: Posture work aims to recover height lost to slouching or an exaggerated lower-back curve and to improve how the torso looks, with the belly and rear less pushed out and the shoulders more open. Believers report gains of an inch or two; the measurable component is the difference between slumped and upright standing height.

paras: Pelvic tilt is the orientation of the pelvis relative to the thigh bones and the rest of the body. Wikipedia defines anterior pelvic tilt as the front of the pelvis dropping relative to the back, linked to shortened hip flexors and lengthened hip extensors, and equates it with an exaggerated lower-back curve (lumbar hyperlordosis). Posterior tilt is the opposite pattern, and lateral tilt is associated with scoliosis or legs of unequal length.[4] Spine surgeons describe pelvic incidence as a fixed anatomical angle, while pelvic tilt and sacral slope are positional and change as the body compensates for spinal curvature.[8][9]

Wikipedia's lordosis article describes the lower-back curve as a normal feature that helps keep body mass over the pelvis, with excessive arching known as hyperlordosis, 'hollow back' or 'saddle back'. It lists weak abdominals and hamstrings, tight hip flexors, extra abdominal fat, pregnancy, prolonged sitting and growth spurts among common contributors, and describes a swayed-back look in which the stomach and buttocks appear pushed out.[15] The same article distinguishes this from slouching, which may only make a person look shorter.[15]

Rib flare, the forward or outward tilt of the lower ribs, is discussed in forum posts as part of the same pattern: when the pelvis tips forward and the lower back arches, the front of the ribcage can sit higher and flare. Practitioners treat it as a companion to pelvic tilt rather than a separate condition.

sections.h: How people use it to look taller and better proportioned
paras: In looksmaxxing, height is hard to change after growth plates close, so posture is the main lever that is free and reversible. The reasoning has two parts. First, standing height as measured depends on how the spine is held and loaded. Wikipedia's height article notes that people measure shorter after exercise or at the end of the day and taller after lying down, and cites a study of 100 children whose height dropped by an average of about 1.5 cm between getting out of bed and late afternoon; it also gives a typical measurement error of about 0.5 cm.[16] Posture advocates read this as evidence that how the trunk is held can move stature by centimetres.

Second, alignment changes how the body reads. Wikipedia's lordosis page notes the swayed-back look of an exaggerated arch and, in a passage tagged as needing citation, states that hyperlordosis can reduce height by roughly 0.5 to 2.5 inches.[15] Posturemaxxing guides on looksmax.org frame forward head and shoulders and APT as common outcomes of desk work and say correcting them makes a person look taller, broader through the shoulders and less belly-forward.[18] The psychology literature summarised on Wikipedia adds that observers use posture to judge confidence and mood, with open, upright postures generally read more favourably.[17]

The methods described in forums and in Wikipedia's pelvic tilt article are ordinary mobility and strength work. For anterior tilt, Wikipedia lists stretching the hip flexors and strengthening the glutes, abdominals and lower back, with glute bridges, planks, side planks, dead bugs and hip thrusts as examples. For posterior tilt it lists strengthening the back extensors and hip extensors while stretching the hip flexors and abdominals. For lateral tilt it points to the cause, such as a heel lift or orthotic for leg-length difference or bracing for structural scoliosis.[4]

A looksmax.org posturemaxxing guide adds upper-body work for forward head and rounded shoulders, including stretching the upper trapezius, neck and chest, chin tucks and wall angels, and tells readers to prioritise form; a reply says the stretches, wall angels and hip flexor work produced a visible difference.[18] A separate thread author credits hip flexor stretching, hip thrusts and abdominal and glute training for growing from 5'11 to 6'1.[3] Practitioners generally describe results arriving over months rather than days, though thread titles also promise a fix in two weeks.[11]

The vocabulary comes from physiotherapy and spine surgery, where pelvic tilt, sacral slope and lordosis are standard measurements.[5][8] Gym and rehabilitation culture popularised the 'lower crossed' pattern of tight hip flexors and weak glutes, and the idea then travelled into height and aesthetics forums, where APT became shorthand for a correctable cause of lost height and a protruding stomach.

On looksmax.org the topic appears across many years of threads, from questions such as whether correcting APT would increase height[10] and how to fix it to regain lost inches,[2] to success stories[3] and a general posturemaxxing guide for desk workers.[18] Other threads ask whether people have beaten APT at all.[20] On T Nation, posture comes up in training logs, where posters discuss hunched shoulders and small presence in tall lifters, and lifters pair mobility drills with lifting.[19]

The vocabulary comes from physiotherapy and spine surgery, where pelvic tilt, sacral slope and lordosis are standard measurements.[5][8] In looksmaxxing forums, APT became shorthand for a possibly correctable cause of lost height and a protruding stomach.

Radiographic work establishes what normal looks like and why it matters clinically. A 2005 study analysed sagittal alignment in asymptomatic volunteers,[13] and adult spinal deformity studies in Spine found that pelvic tilt and truncal inclination relate to patient-reported pain and disability[5] and that spinopelvic parameters correlate with health-related quality of life.[6] A 2024 review reports that anterior pelvic tilt increases hamstring strain and is a factor to target in injury prevention and rehabilitation.[7]

No study located measured whole-body stature before and after pelvic tilt or rib flare correction in healthy people. Wikipedia's pelvic tilt article gives no effectiveness data for its exercise suggestions and carries a reliability tag on one exercise source.[4]

The exercises involved are conventional stretching and strength work, with no specific harms described. Clinicians caution that persistent or asymmetric tilt can be a sign of scoliosis, a leg-length difference or another structural cause, which Wikipedia says are addressed by treating the cause, for example with orthotics or bracing.[4] Severe back problems are a recurring theme in forum threads, including users in their teens reporting back pain and scoliosis alongside APT.[2] Chasing a specific inch gain can lead to disappointment: one poster reports that none of the stretches he does has any effect.[2]

Posture is framed as the accessible half of height maxxing: the part that needs no surgery or drugs. Threads link body alignment to facial symmetry, for example a poster who notes one shoulder sits lower and asks whether pelvic tilt causes facial asymmetry; one reply says body symmetry affects face symmetry, and another says it cannot be changed once present.[1] On T Nation, one poster observes that tall people often have a smaller presence through hunched, slumped posture, a comment that treats posture as part of how height is perceived.[19]

No studies found on pelvic tilt or rib posture correction for increasing stature in healthy people. Related research includes the 2024 meta-analysis of stretching and strengthening for posture,[12] adult spinal deformity studies linking pelvic tilt to pain and disability,[5][6] a 2024 review of anterior pelvic tilt and hamstring injury,[7] and a registered trial of standing trunk extension and spinal height in people with low back pain (NCT03785457), which began in November 2019 with 35 participants.[14]

lore.intro: Posture threads on looksmax.org frame pelvic tilt as lost height, as a cause of asymmetry and as a trait that can be fixed; most reports are personal accounts.[1][2][3][18]

claims.claim: Fixing anterior pelvic tilt can add inches of height.
claims.believers: One poster reports gaining two inches, from 5'11 to 6'1, using hip flexor stretching, hip thrusts and abs and glute training; another thinks he could be one to two inches taller without APT and scoliosis.[3][2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia gives no effectiveness data for tilt exercises and shows the height link only in an image; no study located measured height change after correction.[4]

claims.claim: Pelvic tilt can be fixed with stretching in weeks.
claims.believers: Thread titles promise a fix in two weeks and ask for the best way to regain inches, while another user says his stretches have done nothing.[11][2]
claims.experts: A 2024 meta-analysis of 23 trials found no significant effect of chronic stretching on posture in healthy people and large improvements with chronic strengthening.[12]

claims.claim: Pelvic or shoulder tilt causes facial asymmetry.
claims.believers: A poster links a lower shoulder and pelvis with an asymmetrical face, and a reply says body symmetry affects face symmetry.[1]
claims.experts: No study located tested a link between pelvic tilt and facial asymmetry.

claims.claim: Posture work makes you look taller and broader even without measurable height change.
claims.believers: A posturemaxxing guide says desk work produces forward head, rounded shoulders and APT, and that correcting them improves how the body looks; one reply reports a visible difference from wall angels, chin tucks and hip flexor stretching.[18]
claims.experts: Psychology summaries note that observers read upright, open postures as more confident; the height article notes measurements vary by about 0.5 cm and by time of day.[17][16]

claims.claim: Hyperlordosis shortens stature by up to a couple of inches.
claims.believers: Posters with APT and scoliosis estimate they would be one to two inches taller without it.[2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia's lordosis article states a 0.5 to 2.5 inch loss but tags the claim as needing a citation, and separates it from slouching.[15]

claims.claim: Strengthening works better than stretching for tilt.
claims.believers: Forum guides recommend both stretching hip flexors and strengthening glutes and core.[18][3]
claims.experts: The 2024 meta-analysis found strengthening superior to stretching for posture measures in healthy people.[12]

claims.claim: Anterior pelvic tilt is a health problem as well as an aesthetic one.
claims.believers: Posters describe back problems alongside APT.[2]
claims.experts: A 2024 review reports anterior pelvic tilt increases hamstring strain, and spinal deformity studies link altered pelvic tilt with pain and disability.[7][5]

card.summary: Correcting pelvic tilt and rib flare to recover height; forum anecdotes, but no study measures stature change.
card.note: Pelvic tilt research concerns back pain and spinal deformity, not height.

quick.overview:
Posture for height is the belief that fixing anterior pelvic tilt or rib flare adds centimetres. Forum users report gains of one to two inches after stretching and strengthening.

Clinical literature on pelvic tilt concerns spinal alignment, pain and disability; no study located measured height change.
quick.mechanism: Believers say a tilted pelvis exaggerates the lower-back curve and shortens apparent stature, and that stretching hip flexors while strengthening glutes and core restores it.
quick.risks: The exercises discussed are ordinary mobility and strength work; sources report no specific harms. Persistent tilt asymmetry can relate to scoliosis or leg-length differences, which Wikipedia says are addressed by clinicians.
